content.text:
I found five em dashes and a handful of other AI tells. Most of the copy is in [page.tsx](app/page.tsx), plus a few lines in `layout.tsx` and `StepArt.tsx`.

## Em dashes (5)
- [layout.tsx:9](app/layout.tsx:9): the page title, "Earshot — live AI captions for any video"
- [page.tsx:67](app/page.tsx:67): "…any video that plays in the page — no YouTube captions required."
- [page.tsx:100](app/page.tsx:100): "…press Share — and only that tab."
- [page.tsx:177](app/page.tsx:177): "Captions appear as words are spoken — usually in under a second."
- [StepArt.tsx:56](components/StepArt.tsx:56): "Earshot asks Chrome to listen to this tab — nothing else."

## Other copy smells
- **A dramatic add-on after the dash.** "— and only that tab" and "— nothing else" have the same shape: a point, then an emphatic reassurance tacked on. Together they say the same thing twice.
- **A cute parallel headline.** "Your audio, your call" ([page.tsx:98](app/page.tsx:98)) is a very common AI section title.
- **Lists of three everywhere:**
  - "search, click to jump back, and download" (line 38)
  - "Any YouTube video, Short or livestream" (line 74)
  - "searchable, clickable transcript" in the meta description
- **"No X required"** (line 68) is a stock tagline phrase.
- **Hype filler words:**
  - "right here in Earshot's player" (line 74)
  - "right on youtube.com" (line 112)
  - "ends it instantly" (line 103)
  - "powered by Deepgram Nova-3" in the meta description
- **An overclaim the page then walks back.** The headline says "for **any** video." Line 112 says some videos can't be played outside YouTube, and the footer says it only works in Chrome and Edge on desktop. The "AI" in the headline is also buzzwordy, since nobody picks captions because they're AI.
- **The product as a person.** "Earshot listens along" and "Earshot hears the video" turn the app into a character. "Transcripts live in your browser tab" does the same.
- **The same line twice.** "Paste a YouTube video or livestream" appears in both the hero (line 38) and the meta description.

## Layout and design smells
- **The default AI landing page structure:** a hero with a big headline, a subhead and an input; then a "How it works" section with three numbered steps and illustration cards; then a two-card grid; then a two-item footer.
- **The default styling:** a dark theme with one warm accent color, `rounded-3xl` cards with a 1px ring, a radial gradient behind the preview, and a pulsing "Live captions" badge. Bricolage Grotesque with Inter is also a font pairing that AI tools reach for constantly.
- **Developer instructions in a card for visitors.** The extension card ([page.tsx:115-128](app/page.tsx:115)) gives `npm run build` steps. That reads like a README pasted into the page, not something a visitor can act on.

## What isn't a problem
- The curly quotes and the "Try one:" example chips are fine.
- The caption preview that writes itself in is a real, specific detail. Keep it.

content.text:
Nothing's edited yet. Here's what I'd change each line to, so you can approve or redline first.

**Page title** ([layout.tsx:9](app/layout.tsx:9))
- Before: Earshot — live AI captions for any video
- After: Earshot: live captions for YouTube

**Meta description**
- Before: Paste a YouTube video or livestream and get real-time captions and a searchable, clickable transcript, powered by Deepgram Nova-3.
- After: Live captions and a transcript for YouTube videos and streams that don't have captions.

**Hero headline**
- Before: Live AI captions for any video.
- After: Captions for videos that don't have them.

**Hero subhead**
- Before: Paste a YouTube video or livestream. Earshot listens along and writes captions as people speak, plus a transcript you can search, click to jump back, and download.
- After: Paste a YouTube link and captions show up as people talk. You also get a transcript. Click any line to jump back to that moment.

**How it works intro** (line 67)
- Before: Earshot hears the video through Chrome's tab sharing, so it works with any video that plays in the page — no YouTube captions required.
- After: It uses Chrome's tab sharing to hear the video's audio. The video doesn't need captions of its own.

**Step 1** (line 74)
- Before: Any YouTube video, Short or livestream. It plays right here in Earshot's player.
- After: Videos, Shorts and livestreams all work. The video plays on this page.

**Step 2** ([StepArt.tsx:56](components/StepArt.tsx:56))
- Before: Earshot asks Chrome to listen to this tab — nothing else.
- After: Chrome will ask which tab to share.

**Privacy card heading** (line 98)
- Before: Your audio, your call
- After: Privacy

**Privacy bullets**
- Before: Earshot only hears a tab after you pick it and press Share — and only that tab.
- After: Earshot can only hear the tab you share.
- Before: Audio streams to Deepgram for transcription while captions are on. Stop captions, or Chrome's "Stop sharing", ends it instantly.
- After: While captions are on, the audio goes to Deepgram to be transcribed. Stopping captions, or clicking "Stop sharing" in Chrome, cuts it off.
- Before: Transcripts live in your browser tab and disappear when you close it. Nothing is stored on a server.
- After: Transcripts aren't saved anywhere. Close the tab and they're gone.

**Caption preview note** (line 177)
- Before: Captions appear as words are spoken — usually in under a second.
- After: Captions usually show up less than a second after someone speaks.

**Extension card** (lines 110–128)
- Before: the "Captions on youtube.com itself" heading, a short pitch, then three `npm run build` steps.
- After: keep the heading and one sentence: "Some videos won't play outside YouTube. The Chrome extension captions them on youtube.com." Then add a "Setup instructions" link to the README instead of the build steps.

**Footer:** no change. It's already plain.

Two choices for you:
1. **The headline.** "Captions for videos that don't have them" says why someone would use Earshot. If you'd rather it say what Earshot is, "Live captions for YouTube" is the safer option.
2. **The layout.** These rewrites change the words only. I could also break up the template structure (hero, three steps, two cards), but that's a bigger change.

content.text:
Yes, I can see it. I opened the shot in the browser pane. The preview is an animated, fairly low-resolution image, so small text is blurry, but the layout is clear. (The em dash fix is already pushed to `main` as `6250625`.)

**What the design looks like**
- **Light theme.** It's off-white with soft greens, the opposite of Earshot's dark theme with amber.
- **A floating card layout.** The whole landing page sits inside a rounded white card. Behind it is a full-bleed 3D scene of a grassy hill, with a blurred green glow around the edges.
- **Hero on the left.** It has a big, bold sans-serif headline. The words "AI video" are in a lime-green accent color with a small "+" in front. Below that are a short paragraph, a pill-shaped lime button with a "Watch the tour" link beside it, and a row of overlapping avatars for social proof.
- **Images on the right.** A few rounded photo cards are scattered at slight angles over the landscape, with small avatar bubbles pinned to them. It reads like people collaborating on a canvas.
- **Minimal navigation.** It's a logo, four small links, "Login" and a black pill "Get a demo" button.

**What could carry over to Earshot**
- The light, airy, single-card look would set Earshot apart from the dark template it uses now.
- The scattered image cards could show caption snippets on video frames instead of the static preview.
- The colored phrase in the headline would work if the wording earns it.

**What to watch out for**
- **AI smells of its own.** The paragraph text in the shot (as far as it's readable) has the same tone you're trying to get rid of. The colored "+AI" headline and the avatar row are also common Dribbble tropes. I'd take the visual direction, not the copy.
- **It's a mockup, not a working page.** The 3D landscape would need a real image or video asset.
- **It's someone else's work.** Kris Anfalova designed it. Using it as inspiration for direction and mood is fine. Copying it pixel for pixel isn't.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rizelscarlett/.claude/skills/frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

{/* Privacy + extension */}

Your audio, your call

  • Earshot only hears a tab after you pick it and press Share, and it only hears that tab.
  • Audio streams to Deepgram for transcription while captions are on. Stop captions, or Chrome’s “Stop sharing”, ends it instantly.
  • Transcripts live in your browser tab and disappear when you close it. Nothing is stored on a server.

Captions on youtube.com itself

Some videos can’t be played outside YouTube. The Earshot Chrome extension captions them right on youtube.com, with a side panel transcript.

content.text:
I've applied the Dribbble shot's ideas to the Earshot home page, and it's running in the browser pane. I checked it at desktop width and on a phone-sized screen, with no console errors. The page typechecks and the watch page still loads. Nothing is committed.

**What I took from the shot**
- **Light theme.** The home page now uses off-white and soft greens instead of near-black and amber.
- **A white card on a landscape.** The hero sits in a rounded white card. Behind it is a pale sky over layered green hills, drawn in code, and the hills show along the right side.
- **Tilted media cards across the card's edge.** In Earshot's version they're captioned videos instead of stock photos:
  - The TED stage, with its caption writing in word by word as before.
  - A small livestream card with a red "Live" badge and the caption "[soft piano music]". Captions describe sound too, not just speech.
  - A transcript card searched for "creativity", with the match highlighted.
- **Pill buttons** and a dark "Chrome extension" button in the top right.

**Where I went my own way**
- **No colored "+AI" word in the headline.** That's one of the tells you're trying to get rid of.
- **No avatar row**, since Earshot has no users to show off.
- **A different font.** The home page now uses Atkinson Hyperlegible Next. It was designed to be easy to read for people with low vision, which suits a captioning tool.

**How it's built**
- The light theme is scoped with a `.theme-field` class in [globals.css](src/app/globals.css). It flips the shared color variables to light, so the URL box, logo and step illustrations restyle themselves.
- The watch page and the Chrome extension keep the dark theme. Video players read better on dark backgrounds.
- The new hero is in [page.tsx](src/app/page.tsx), in `Hills` and `HeroScatter`.

**Not changed yet**
- The copy, apart from the em dashes you already removed.
- The structure below the hero ("How it works" and the two cards). It just picks up the light colors.
- The browser theme color in `layout.tsx` is still dark, so the browser bar on phones will look dark against the light page.

content.text:
You're right, that first pass was lazy. I only looked at a still image of the shot, copied its light look, and didn't check spacing or framing carefully. I threw all of it out and started again from the dark version you had. This time I played the shot's 7-second video frame by frame and worked from its animation and layout, not its colors or words.

The new version is open in the browser pane. Nothing is committed.

**What I took from the shot**
- **Layout: one scene with the text panel floating inside it.** On desktop the hero is a single dark video stage. The headline, link box and example links sit on a solid black panel inside its left half. The right half is the "video": a speaker under a spotlight.
- **Animation: the scene builds itself in order,** like things being placed on a canvas one at a time:

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rizelscarlett/.claude/skills/frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

content.text:
I've rebuilt the hero on your reference's layout in dark mode. It's open in the browser pane. Nothing is committed.

**Left side (the panel)**
- A solid black panel inside a dimly lit stage. The Earshot logo sits top left, with "How it works" and "Privacy" beside it.
- Below that, the headline, the subhead, and the "Paste a YouTube link" box with the "Watch with captions" button.
- "Or try one" sits at the bottom of the panel, where your reference has its team row. Each example has a round icon, like the avatars in the reference: a play button for the TED talk and a pulsing red dot for the livestream.
- A light "Get the Chrome extension" button sits top right, where the reference has "Get a demo".

**Right side (real pieces of Earshot)**
- **Video frame:** the captions write in word by word, with a "Live captions" badge and a progress bar. A round amber sound meter is pinned to its corner, like the avatar circles in the reference.
- **Chrome extension popup:** copied from the real popup, showing the Live badge, "AI captions" switched on, and "Captioning this tab on youtube.com". It's tilted slightly, like the overlapping photo in your reference.
- **Transcript:** timestamped lines with the current one in amber, plus a search box at the bottom, like the reference's message box.
- **Player controls:** the same buttons as the watch page (Stop captions, captions, transcript, fullscreen).

They come in one at a time when the page loads: the stage comes into focus, then the panel, video, controls, popup and transcript. With reduced motion turned on, everything shows without animating.

**Responsive**

| Width | Layout |
|---|---|
| 1280px and up | The full split layout, like your reference |
| 1024 to 1279px | Panel content on top. Below it, video and controls on the left, and popup and transcript in a column on the right, like the real watch page |
| Tablet | The popup and transcript sit side by side under the video |
| Phone | Everything stacks, and the popup overlaps the bottom of the video a little |

I checked phone, tablet, 1024, 1280 and 1440 widths. Nothing runs off the side, there are no console errors, and it typechecks.

**Also changed**
- The fix for the double outline on the focused link box is still in place.
- The privacy section now has an anchor so the new "Privacy" link scrolls to it.

The work is in [page.tsx](src/app/page.tsx) (`HeroProduct`, `VideoFrame`, `ExtensionPopup`, `TranscriptCard`, `PlayerControls`) and the backdrop styles in [globals.css](src/app/globals.css).

content.text:
The home page now fills exactly one screen, the nav links swap the left panel like tabs, and the demo on the right works. Nothing is committed yet.

**Full screen and tabs**
- On wide screens (1280px and up) the stage fills the whole browser window with no scrolling. The sections and footer that used to sit below the hero are gone.
- "How it works", "Privacy" and the "Get the Chrome extension" button now replace the panel's content instead of scrolling down to it. The Earshot logo takes you back to the start. The active tab gets an amber underline.
- Each tab has its own web address (`/#how`, `/#privacy`, `/#extension`), so you can link straight to one.
- On phones and tablets the panel sits on top with the demo below it, and the tabs still swap the panel.
- The footer line ("Earshot is open source…") moved into the Privacy tab.
- On very wide screens like your 2000px one, the headline and the demo cards get a bit bigger so the stage doesn't look empty.

**Interactive demo**
I split the demo into separate pieces that share one pretend video. Three subagents each made one part clickable while I built the tabs, and I tested the result in the browser.
- **Video:** captions write in word by word in time with the video. Click the video to pause or play it. Click or drag the progress bar to jump around; arrow keys work too.
- **Extension popup:** the on/off switch works. Turning it off stops the captions on the video, changes the badge to "Off", and shows the real popup's "Turn on to caption…" message.
- **Transcript:** new lines appear as they're spoken. Clicking a line jumps the video there. Search highlights matching words, and Download saves a .txt file.
- **Controls:** Stop/Start captions stays in sync with the popup switch. CC hides the captions, the transcript button hides the transcript card, and full screen enlarges the whole demo.
- When captions are off, the sound meter stops moving.
- The talk in the demo is made up, so it doesn't quote the real TED talk.

**Two notes**
- I left the hydration warning alone, as you asked. It appears because your ColorZilla extension adds an attribute to the page.
- I checked phone, 1024, 1280, 1440 and 1920 widths. Nothing runs off the side and it typechecks. I didn't try the full screen button, because the test browser can't enter full screen without a real click.

The new files are [HeroPanel.tsx](apps/web/src/components/HeroPanel.tsx) and everything in [hero-demo/](apps/web/src/components/hero-demo/). [page.tsx](apps/web/src/app/page.tsx) now just puts the two together.

content.text:
I've rebuilt the page so it uses the space better, with fewer words and bigger type. Nothing is committed yet.

**Fewer words, bigger type**
- **Privacy:** cut down to three short points, each a bold line plus one sentence:
  - Only the tab you pick
  - Only to Deepgram, only while on
  - Nothing is saved
- **How it works:** three numbered steps with one short line each.
- **Chrome extension:** three steps, with the commands in small code boxes.
- The home subhead went from 30 words to 21.
- All three tabs now sit vertically centered in the panel like the home tab, instead of hanging off the top with a big empty space below. A short footer line sits at the bottom where "Or try one" sits on home.
- On wide screens like yours (2000px) the type is bigger: an 84px headline, larger nav, and larger body text.

**Using the space**
- The demo is now one composed product, laid out like the real watch page: the video with the transcript beside it at the same height, the player controls under the video, and the extension popup under the transcript.
- The left panel is a little narrower on wide screens, so the video gets more width. At 2000px it's about twice the size it was.
- Nothing floats loose in the corners anymore.

**Checks**
- I checked phone, 1024, 1280, 1440 and 2000px widths. Nothing runs off the side, and it typechecks.
- I fixed two problems I found along the way: on phones the video had disappeared, and at 1280 the transcript overflowed its card.
- At 1280 to 1440 the demo is still on the small side, because the panel needs room for the headline and link box.

content.text:
The problem with "Your audio, your call" is that it's a slogan. It's catchy, but it doesn't tell you anything. The three points under it already say exactly what happens, so the headline should state the main fact plainly. Some options:

1. **Earshot only hears what you share.** This is my pick. It's the strongest promise on the page and leads straight into the three points.
2. **It only hears the tab you pick.** More specific, but it repeats the first point word for word.
3. **What happens to your audio.** Plain, and it frames the tab as answers. It reads more like a help-page heading than a promise.
4. **Nothing is kept.** Short and bold, but it only covers the third point.
5. **Privacy.** The same as the tab name. Honest, but flat next to "Live AI captions for any video."

If you go with 1, I'd also cut the line under it ("Earshot only listens when you ask, and keeps nothing.") because the headline would already say it. The three points would then follow straight after.

Which one do you want, or is there a direction I'm missing?

I think that works, as long as the three points take over the headline's job. The nav already shows "Privacy" underlined, so a heading saying it again isn't needed.

Here's how I'd do it:
- **Drop the headline and the line under it.**
- **Make the three point titles big,** about 36–44px in the display font, so each one reads as a headline:
  - **Only the tab you pick.**
  - **Only to Deepgram, only while on.**
  - **Nothing is saved.**
- **Keep the one plain sentence under each title,** so the reasons are still there.

The tab then reads as three strong statements stacked in the middle of the panel. It's punchier than a headline over small print, and it fills the space better.

The catch is consistency: How it works and Chrome extension would still have headlines. Those two need them more, though, since steps need a title to read as a sequence. So I'd only drop the headline on Privacy.

Want me to make that change?

The Privacy tab no longer has a headline. The three promises are now the headlines, set in the large display font with one plain sentence under each:

- **Only the tab you pick.** Nothing is heard until you choose a tab and press Share.
- **Only to Deepgram, only while on.** Audio goes to Deepgram for captions and stops when you stop.

I checked it at 2000px, 1280px and phone width. Nothing is committed yet.

content.text:
I fixed both tabs: smaller, steadier type, no more collision with the nav, and a gentler focus outline.

**How it works**
- **The overlap.** The panel was too short for everything in this tab, so it pushed the title up into the nav. I made the whole tab more compact: the title drops from 64px to 48px (60px on very wide screens), the pictures and step text are smaller, and the steps sit closer together. There's now always at least 32px between the nav and the title.
- **Pictures.** Labels inside them ("Start captions", "This tab") no longer wrap onto two lines. On phones the pictures are hidden, because at that size they were too small to read.

**Privacy**
- **Size.** The three statements are smaller, so they read as a calm list rather than three competing headlines: 28px on phones, 32px on desktop, 40px on very wide screens.
- **Spacing.** Each sentence underneath sits tighter to its statement, and thin lines separate the three.

**Nav focus box**
- The square outline around the active tab now has rounded corners and sits further from the text, so it no longer looks boxed in.
- I didn't find out why it shows up after a mouse click.

I checked both tabs at 1280×720, 1440×800 (which looks close to your screen) and 2000px wide, plus phone width. Both fit the panel at every desktop size with no overflow, and the type check passes. Nothing is committed.

+Heard is an open-source web video player and Chrome extension. They add real-time captions and an interactive transcript to online video using **Deepgram Nova-3** streaming speech-to-text. They don't depend on the video platform's own captions.

- **Web platform** (`apps/web`, Next.js): paste a YouTube video or livestream URL and watch it with live captions, plus a searchable transcript with timestamps you can download and click to jump in the video.

content.text:
"Earshot" no longer appears anywhere in the code. The only exception is one new file, which needs the old name to find saved settings. All three packages type-check, the tests pass (30 passed, 2 skipped), and the extension builds; its built manifest is named "Heard — Live AI Captions". Nothing is committed.

**What changed**
- **Packages:** `@earshot/shared`, `/web` and `/extension` are now `@heard/…`, and the root package is `heard`. The lockfile is refreshed to match.
- **Environment variables:** they now start with `HEARD_` instead of `EARSHOT_`, for example `HEARD_EXTENSION_IDS` and `WXT_HEARD_URL`. In your `apps/web/.env.local` I renamed only the variable name and left its value alone.
- **CSS and code names:** classes, the caption animation, the audio processor and log prefixes now use "heard".
- **Saved browser settings:** these keys now start with `heard:` too. A new file, `apps/web/src/lib/legacy-storage.ts`, moves any old `earshot:` keys over once on first load, so nobody loses a saved Deepgram key or caption style. I tested this on the watch page and both test settings carried over.

**Two things to know**
- **Vercel:** if you set any `EARSHOT_*` variables there, rename them to `HEARD_*` in the dashboard. The app no longer reads the old names.
- **Your PATH:** the first `node` on it is the copy bundled with ChatGPT.app. It can't load native modules, so the tests, the extension build and the dev server all failed with it. That happens with or without the rename. I set `.claude/launch.json` to start the dev server with your nvm Node (v22.23.1) instead, and that path is specific to your machine.

**Demo on the right**
- **Tilt:** the transcript leans 1.5°, the extension popup 2.5° the other way, and the controls 1°. The video stays straight so the rest has something to lean against.
- **Entrance:** the pieces now arrive one at a time: video, then controls, transcript, and the extension popup last, about 0.6 seconds apart. Each slides up from slightly out of focus. They already arrived in order before, but the motion was so small it was easy to miss.
- **Balance:** the group was sitting low with empty space above it. It's now centered in the stage, and the controls line up with the middle of the popup instead of hugging the top.

**How it works**
- **Tilt:** the three pictures alternate tilts, so they look like pieces laid on the page.
- **Entrance:** the steps appear one after another when you open the tab.
- **"Paste a link" button:** I removed the big amber button. Step 1 now ends with a small amber "Paste one now" link, which goes to the home tab where you paste it.

If someone has reduced motion turned on, nothing animates. At 1280×720 everything still fits without overflowing. I also deleted a block of CSS in `globals.css` that appeared twice. Nothing is committed.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rizelscarlett/.claude/skills/frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

content.text:
I rebuilt the demo as one composed scene instead of a tidy grid:

- **Video:** it's the anchor. "Live captions" moved to its top-left on wide screens so the transcript doesn't crowd it.
- **Controls:** the bar was the full width of the video; now it's a compact pill again, straddling the video's bottom edge the way the prostex toolbar sits on its scene. The Stop captions button and icons are bigger than they were originally, and the caption sits higher so the pill doesn't cover it.
- **Transcript:** it starts higher than the video, tucks slightly over its right edge, and leans 2°.
- **Extension popup:** it drops in below the transcript, leaning the other way, so the eye moves from video to transcript to popup.

On desktop the pieces sit on a fixed 760×560 layout that scales to fit the space. The arrangement looks the same at 1280, 1440 and 2000 wide; only the size changes. On phones and tablets they stack in a centered column: video, controls, transcript, then the popup slightly overlapping it.

They still arrive one at a time, and everything stays interactive. I checked phone, 1024, 1280, 1440 and 2000 widths: there's no sideways scrolling, and the type check passes. Nothing is committed yet.

content.text:
There are seven layouts to choose from on the home page now. On a desktop-width window, a switcher at the bottom of the demo flips between them. You can also open one directly, for example `127.0.0.1:3100/?layout=3`. All seven are taller than they are wide, and every piece is tilted:

1. **Cascade:** the video sits on top with the controls hanging off it. The popup is below on the left and the transcript below on the right.
2. **Stack:** the transcript is at the top right, then the video, then the popup at the bottom right.
3. **Tower:** the video is on top. The popup and transcript sit side by side underneath, tilted in opposite directions.
4. **Fan:** the video is tilted most, at -3°. The transcript and popup fan out below it, left and right.
5. **Pinned:** the popup is pinned at the top right above the video. A wide, short transcript sits below.
6. **Zigzag:** the video is at the top left, the transcript below it on the right, and the popup on the left. Your eye zigzags down the page.
7. **Diagonal:** the pieces step down from top left to bottom right: video, then transcript, then popup.

Every piece still works: play/pause, seeking, search and the popup switch. Once you pick one, I'll delete the other six and the switcher. I can also make that layout tilt more if you'd like. Nothing is committed yet.

Agreed. With a tall diagonal, the demo doesn't need half the screen. In your screenshot it only fills the middle strip of the stage: about 200px is empty between the panel and the video, and more sits to the right of the popup. Its size is limited by the stage's height (the layout is 760px tall), so the spare width just goes unused.

Here's what I'd do:

1. **Give the panel more of the screen.** Widen the left panel from 46% of the width to about 52–54%. That leaves the demo a narrower column that fits its tall shape. The headline and steps get more room, and How it works stops looking crammed into the left half.
2. **Tighten the diagonal.** Close the gaps between the steps so the transcript overlaps the video's controls a little and the popup overlaps the transcript's bottom corner. It reads more as one cluster, and because it's shorter it can scale up a bit.

That keeps the diagonal look but makes it feel deliberate instead of floating in a wide, empty space.

Want me to do both, or did you mean a different area by "here"?

2. **Key Technical Concepts**
   - **Stack**
     - Next.js 16 (Turbopack) with Tailwind v4 and the Bricolage Grotesque and Inter fonts.
     - Monorepo:
       - `apps/web` (`@heard/web`)
       - `apps/extension` (`@heard/extension`, built with WXT)
       - `packages/shared` (`@heard/shared`)
   - **Node environment problem.** The first `node` on PATH is ChatGPT.app's hardened copy, which can't load native modules (lightningcss, rolldown, next-swc fail with "different Team IDs").
     - Fix in the shell: `PATH=$HOME/.nvm/versions/node/v22.23.1/bin:$PATH`.

   - **Tailwind gotchas.**
     - Two base display utilities on one element (`hidden` and `inline-flex`) conflict unpredictably. Use a wrapper span instead.
     - Variant utilities (`@[23rem]:inline`) do override base ones.
     - `grid-cols-subgrid` works.

     - On xl screens the demo is a fixed-pixel canvas, scaled with a CSS variable `--demo-scale` that a ResizeObserver hook sets.
     - Pieces are positioned through CSS variables (`--x`, `--y`, `--w`, `--h`, `--r`) with arbitrary-value classes such as `xl:left-[var(--x)]` and `xl:rotate-[var(--r)]`.

     - Keep `next dev` on 127.0.0.1.

     - Don't loosen the token endpoint's CORS, rate limit or origin checks without the owner's say-so.
     - Read `docs/provider-policies.md` before changing how YouTube content is shown or captured.
     - If the owner explicitly chooses to pay for visitors, also set `HEARD_EXTENSION_IDS`.

     - Commit and push only when asked.

     - Panel width is `xl:w-[calc(52%-1rem)] 2xl:w-[calc(48%-1rem)]`.

       - Privacy step art (`SendArt` etc.).

     - The layout constant:

content.text:
Three of your four already exist. [settings.ts](packages/shared/src/core/settings.ts) and [CaptionSettingsForm.tsx](packages/shared/src/react/CaptionSettingsForm.tsx) give you six sizes, four text colors and sans/serif/mono fonts. They also cover background style and opacity, the number of lines, and over-video or below-video placement.

The real work is in two places:
- **Bold:** the caption weight is hard-coded at 500 in [CaptionText.tsx](packages/shared/src/react/CaptionText.tsx).
- **Language:** Deepgram is always asked for English, set in [deepgram.ts:11](packages/shared/src/core/deepgram.ts:11).

## What you're leaving out

**Languages (the biggest gap)**
- **Transcribing vs translating.** Deepgram writes down what's spoken, in the language it's spoken in. Showing Spanish audio as English captions needs a separate translation service, which is another paid key. Under the "who pays" rules in AGENTS.md, that needs your own decision.
- **Auto-detect and mixed languages.** Nova-3 has a `multi` mode for speakers who switch languages mid-sentence. That's often a better default than making people pick.
- **Changing language mid-session** means reconnecting to Deepgram, so the UI has to handle a short gap.
- **Right-to-left scripts** (Arabic, Hebrew) need `dir="rtl"`. Japanese, Chinese and Korean need font fallbacks, because the mono and serif stacks won't cover them.
- **Formatting support varies by language.** Smart punctuation and number formatting aren't available everywhere.

**Readability**
- **Text outline or drop shadow.** This is the standard alternative to a background box. TV captions offer raised, depressed, uniform and drop-shadow styles.
- **Custom colors.** Today there are only four text color presets, and no background color choice.
- **A contrast warning** when someone picks, say, yellow text on no background over a bright video.
- **Line spacing and all-caps or sentence case.**

**Behavior**
- **A live preview** in the settings panel, so people see changes without a video playing.
- **Turning off the word-by-word reveal and fade** for people who find motion distracting.
- **Speaker labels** using Deepgram's diarization, such as "Speaker 1:".
- **A profanity filter** and custom vocabulary for names and jargon (Deepgram's keyterms).

**Persistence**
- **Saved presets**, such as "Lecture" or "Movie night".
- **Sync across devices** with `chrome.storage.sync`.
- **Per-site overrides.**

## How subagents would split it

Each lane gets its own files so two agents never edit the same one:

1. **Settings model (goes first, because everything depends on it):** add `fontWeight`, `language` and any new fields to `types.ts`. Also update `normalizeCaptionSettings`, with tests in `packages/shared/test`.
2. **Language pipeline:** pass the language through `deepgram.ts` and `session.ts`, reconnect when it changes, and keep a list of Nova-3 languages.
3. **Caption rendering:** `CaptionText.tsx` handles weight, outline or shadow, RTL text and font fallbacks.
4. **Settings UI:** `CaptionSettingsForm.tsx` gets the new controls and a live preview, wired into the web settings popover and the extension side panel.
5. **Verification (runs last):** run the tests, check the web player in the browser, and rebuild the extension.

Lanes 2–4 can run in parallel once lane 1 lands.

api/SKILL.md:170:| Best for | Existing Aura integrations, English–Spanish codeswitching voices, non-English voices inside a Voice Agent, compressed audio inside a Voice Agent | Voice agents — streaming LLM output, barge-in, multi-turn conversations |
api/SKILL.md:260:16. **Use `/v2/listen` and a `flux-general-*` model.** Two are served: `flux-general-en` (English) and `flux-general-multi` (multilingual, and the only `/v2/listen` model that accepts `language_hint` / `language_hints`; on `/v1/listen`, `language_hint` biases Nova-3 `language=multi`). `/v1/listen` does not support Flux STT, and `model=flux` alone is not a valid value. Do not include `language` or `encoding` params for containerized audio.
api/SKILL.md:262:17. **Use `Configure` to update EOT thresholds, keyterms, language hints, and `numerals` mid-session.** Unlike `/v1/listen`, Flux STT supports live reconfiguration after connection, so there is no need to reconnect to change turn detection sensitivity, boost new keyterms, re-bias language detection (`language_hints`, `flux-general-multi` only), or switch `numerals` on for a PIN or order number:
api/SKILL.md:276:20. **`language` is required on `/v1/read`, and it is validated before anything else.** There is no default: omitting it returns `400 INVALID_QUERY_PARAMETER` with the message "Failed to deserialize query parameters: missing field `language`", which masks every other problem in the request. English only: `language=multi` is rejected, and `en-US` is accepted but echoed back as `en`. Two more `/v1/read` shapes worth knowing: the JSON body takes **exactly one** of `text` or `url` (both or neither gives `PAYLOAD_ERROR`, and `url` must point at a plain-text document, since audio gives `REMOTE_CONTENT_ERROR`), and it is POST-only (`GET` and a WebSocket upgrade both return 405). `summarize` on `/v1/read` accepts `v2` as well as `true`. Result paths differ per endpoint: `/v1/read` returns `results.summary.text`, `/v1/listen` returns `results.summary.short`, so code that handles both has to branch. The search didn't turn up a published end-to-end latency figure for the DeepL Voice API. What it did show:

- **Architecture:** The Voice API transcribes and translates audio over a WebSocket connection. The flow requests a streaming URL via POST, then streams audio and text via WebSocket. Session resumption after a dropped connection is supported.
- **Latency approach:** DeepL's research paper says real-time speech translation has an inherent tension between translation quality and low latency. DeepL says it starts translating before sentences finish, and that its models handle real-time audio end-to-end, with no handoffs to different APIs.
- **Specific numbers:** The only figure I found is a marketing claim from a DeepL blog post about the Mixhalo partnership, describing a 500-millisecond time saving in the speed a spoken translation reaches its audience. That is a relative improvement, not a total latency measurement.
- **Availability:** Per the docs, speech-to-text and speech-to-speech are available to all customers with a paid DeepL API subscription. Speech-to-speech is listed as closed beta in the API reference.
- **Glossaries:** Glossary terms are matched against the source transcription as it's produced, not against a complete text, which matters for streaming use.

For a real latency number, the DeepL Voice Research paper (IJCAI 2026) and the Real-Time Voice Quickstart on developers.deepl.com are the best next sources to check.

Chrome's Translator API is in Chrome Stable as of Chrome 144, but the language list I found is incomplete and may be out of date.

- **Stable status:** A January 2026 Chrome blog post says as of Chrome 144, the Translator API is supported, along with all of the other built-in AI APIs. It adds that this API is in Chrome Stable, so it works on Chromebook Plus and on desktop macOS, Windows, and Linux.
- **Platform limits:** The API is desktop-only. The Language Detector and Translator APIs work in Chrome on desktop. These APIs don't work on mobile devices.
- **Model delivery:** The model is not bundled. The API is built into Chrome, and the model is downloaded the first time a website uses this API. Developers check status with the asynchronous Translator.availability() function. Per the developer guidance, availability returns one of four string statuses, and the 'available' status means the pair is already on the device.
- **Languages:** The language-support lists I found are from an older snapshot. One version, last updated May 20, 2025 and Chrome 138, lists codes including ar, bg, bn, cs, da, de, el, en, es, fi, fr, hi, hr, continuing through uk, vi, zh, and zh-Hant. The snippets I retrieved don't show the full current list, so check the live Translator API page for the current set of supported languages.

content.text:
You were right that I hadn't searched enough. I looked again, and the answer about Deepgram still holds: its 2026 changelog covers new languages and multilingual transcription, but not translation. Some third-party posts claim Deepgram has translation, but they contradict themselves. The iTranslate post is from 2022 and sends finished lines to a separate translation service. So the real question is which translation service to use alongside Deepgram.

## The options

| Approach | Cost | Fit for Heard |
|---|---|---|
| **Chrome's built-in Translator API** | Free, on-device | **Best fit.** It's in stable Chrome since version 144 and needs no key. Text never leaves the browser, which matches how Heard handles keys. The extension is Chrome-only anyway. Downsides: desktop only, and each language pair downloads on first use. |
| **DeepL text API, user's own key** | Free tier, then paid | **Good fallback** for the web app in other browsers, and the strongest translation quality. It would follow the same bring-your-own-key pattern as Deepgram. |
| **Switch to a provider with translation built in** (Soniox, Speechmatics, AssemblyAI, DeepL Voice) | Paid per hour | They return translated captions natively. But that means replacing Deepgram, which is a rewrite. |
| **Speech-to-speech** (OpenAI gpt-realtime-translate, Gemini Live) | About $0.035/min | Wrong output: these return translated audio, not captions. |

## Recommendation

Keep Deepgram for transcription, using `language=multi` so it detects the spoken language. Translate each finished line with Chrome's Translator. While a line is still being spoken, show it in the original language, then swap in the translation when it's final. Add DeepL with the user's own key only as a fallback when Chrome's Translator isn't available.

Sources:
- [Deepgram changelog, Oct 5 2026](https://developers.deepgram.com/changelog/2026/10/5)
- [Deepgram changelog, Sep 3 2026](https://developers.deepgram.com/changelog/2026/9/3)
- [Deepgram: Adding Translation (iTranslate)](https://deepgram.com/learn/translation-itranslate)
- [Third-party post on Nova-3 Multilingual (contradicts itself)](https://callsphere.ai/blog/vw1a-deepgram-nova-3-multilingual-march-2026-wer-drop)
- [AssemblyAI: Best real-time speech translation APIs in 2026](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/best-real-time-speech-translation-apis)
- [MarkTechPost: Top 12 AI live translation tools 2026](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/10/12/top-12-ai-live-translation-tools-2026/)
- [Chrome: Translation with built-in AI](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/translator-api)
- [Chrome: built-in AI in Chrome 144](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/ai-translation-chromebook-plus)
- [DeepL Voice API overview](https://developers.deepl.com/docs/voice/overview)

content.text:
Yes, exactly. Deepgram writes down what it hears, in the language it's spoken in. It doesn't change the language.

- **Transcription (Deepgram does this):** someone speaks Spanish and you get Spanish text. Someone speaks Japanese and you get Japanese text. That works in about 50 languages. With `language=multi`, it even follows a speaker who switches between English and Spanish mid-sentence and writes each part in the language spoken.
- **Translation (Deepgram doesn't do this):** someone speaks Spanish and you get English text. That needs a second step that takes the Spanish text and rewrites it in English.

So for Heard:

1. **"Captions in the video's language"** (a French video gets French captions): Deepgram alone handles it. This is the "support for various languages" item on your list.
2. **"Captions in my language"** (a French video gets English captions): Deepgram writes the French, then a translator converts it. That's where Chrome's built-in translator comes in. It runs inside the browser for free, so users don't need another key.

Both use the same Deepgram connection. Translation is just an extra step on the text before it's shown. Want me to build both that way?

content.text:
No. Heard always asks Deepgram for English. In [deepgram.ts:11](packages/shared/src/core/deepgram.ts:11) the language defaults to `"en"`, and nothing in the web app or the extension ever passes a different one.

So if you play a Spanish or Japanese video today, Deepgram tries to hear English and produces garbled captions.

Fixing this is the first piece of the language work:
- Switch the default to `language=multi`, so Deepgram detects the language itself.
- Let users pick a specific language, which is more accurate when they know what the video is in.

It's a small change on its own: one setting plus passing it through to the session.

content.text:
Both pieces are built: Deepgram can now caption any language, and Chrome's built-in translator can turn those captions into another language. I haven't tried either with real speech yet.

**What you'll see:** settings now has a **Language** section with two pickers, in both the web player and the extension side panel.
- **Spoken in the video:** "Detect automatically" is the default. Heard asks Deepgram for `language=multi`, which detects the language and follows speakers who switch mid-sentence. Picking a specific language, such as Spanish, is more accurate. Changing it during a session reconnects to Deepgram without losing audio.
- **Show captions in:** "The spoken language" is the default, so Spanish speech gets Spanish captions. Pick English and each caption is translated on the device, so the text never leaves the browser and there's no extra key or cost.

**How translation behaves:**
- The live caption is translated while it's being spoken, always working on the newest words. If a translation hasn't come back yet, the caption shows the original words in the meantime.
- In the transcript, each line shows the translation with the original in smaller text underneath, and search matches both.
- Chrome downloads each language pair once, and only starts that download from a click. Picking languages in settings starts it, with a progress percentage. If auto-detect hears a language that hasn't been downloaded, a "Download" link appears under the transcript.
- In browsers without the translator, captions stay in the spoken language and settings explains why.
- Right-to-left text, such as Arabic or Hebrew, now displays the right way round.

**Checked:** typecheck passes, and there are 9 new tests (39 passing in total). The extension is rebuilt, so reload Heard in `chrome://extensions`. In the browser pane, the pickers render and the setting is saved. That pane's translator never responds, so I added a 4-second timeout so translation falls back to the original captions instead of freezing.

**Not yet checked:**
- A real Spanish video end to end. That needs actual audio capture and real desktop Chrome, which my browser pane can't do.
- Whether translation works when the extension's side panel is closed. I couldn't test the translator inside the extension, where translation runs on its hidden audio-capture page and the download link lives in the side panel.

**Uncommitted work that isn't mine:** the folder also has edits to `layout.tsx`, `page.tsx` and `HeroPanel.tsx`, plus new `i18n/`, `proxy.ts` and `LanguagePicker.tsx` files. That looks like separate work translating the site itself, and it's why the page title showed in Spanish. I'd leave those files out of this commit.

content.text:
I haven't committed anything, because the language work can't be separated cleanly from the other work in this folder.

Someone else, probably another session, is translating the site's own text into other languages. That work has gone into the same files as mine, including ones I wrote:
- **My new `LanguageSettings.tsx`** now has their label changes in it.
- **These files have both their changes and mine:** `CaptionSettingsForm.tsx`, `TranscriptView.tsx`, `WatchExperience.tsx`, the extension's side panel `App.tsx`, and `react/index.ts`.
- **Their changes depend on new files** (`i18n/`, `labels.ts`, `useSharedLabels.ts`). If I commit only my parts, I'd be committing a version neither of us has run, and it might not even typecheck.

There are three ways to go:
1. **Commit everything together** as one commit covering both caption languages and the translated site. I'd typecheck and run the tests on the combined state first. This is the safest, as long as that other work is ready to commit.
2. **Wait** for the other work to finish and be committed, then commit the language work on top.
3. **Split them by hand.** This is possible, but fiddly and error-prone while the other work is still changing those files.

- Localize the web app (en, es, fr, de, pt, ja) with a language picker.

  README line, smaller hints. README explains finding the hidden folder.
