Base directory for this skill: /Users/rizelscarlett/.claude/skills/frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

content.text:
Caption settings now open in the right sidebar instead of dropping below the controls, so you no longer have to scroll to find them.

- **Desktop:** the settings button swaps the transcript for a **Settings** panel. You can watch the captions change while you adjust them. Close it with the X, Escape, or the transcript button.
- **Phone:** settings slide up as a bottom sheet over the page.
- **Fullscreen:** settings open as a panel beside the video, as before.

I checked desktop and phone sizes in the browser. Nothing is committed.

**On moving the control bar above the video:** I think it's worth trying, and I lean yes.
- **Why it helps:** right now the order is video, then captions, then controls, so the captions get squeezed between the picture and the buttons. With the bar on top, the order becomes title and Start, then the video, then the captions directly underneath. The captions are what you're reading, so they should sit flush against the picture. The bar would also read as a header for the video, with the title and Start button where you look first.
- **The cost:** almost every video player puts its controls below, so it's a little less familiar. Opening settings from the sidebar no longer depends on where the bar is, so this is purely a layout choice.

content.text:
# Plan: translate the Heard extension's interface

**Goal:** the popup, side panel and on-page caption box appear in the same six languages as the website (English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, German, Japanese). By default they follow Chrome's language, and you can change it in the side panel's settings.

**What's already in place:** the shared components (transcript, toolbar, status badge, caption settings, language pickers) already accept translated labels. The web app already has those labels in all six languages, but they live in `apps/web/src/i18n/messages/*/watch.ts` under `ui`, where the extension can't import them.

## Steps

**1. Move the shared translations into the shared package (do this first).**
- Move the `ui` label sets, plus the language list and language names, from `apps/web` to `packages/shared/src/i18n/`.
- The web app imports them from there, so nothing changes for the website.
- This covers roughly half of the extension's text for free.

**2. Add the extension's own text (about 60 strings).**
- Create `apps/extension/i18n/en.ts` with every string written in the popup (13), side panel (28), caption box (10) and background (9).
- That includes the key setup, start/stop, "Hide captions", drag hints, toolbar tooltips and errors.
- The other five languages are typed against the English file, so a missing string fails the typecheck.

**3. Choose the language.**
- Save a `uiLanguage` setting in `chrome.storage.local`. Empty means "follow Chrome", which uses `chrome.i18n.getUILanguage()` matched to the six languages.
- Add a hook (`useUiLanguage` plus `useT`) that the popup, side panel and caption box all use. They listen for storage changes, so switching language updates every open view at once, like the caption settings do today.
- Add an "Interface language" picker in the side panel's Settings.

**4. Fix the background's error messages.**
- Today the background sends finished English sentences, and the side panel detects key errors by matching the text against a pattern (`isKeyError`).
- Switch to error codes plus details, such as `needs_key` with the server URL, and have each view write the sentence in its own language. That removes the fragile pattern match.

**5. The extension's name and description in the Chrome Web Store and `chrome://extensions`.**
- Add `public/_locales/<lang>/messages.json` and set `default_locale: "en"`.
- Chrome uses `pt_BR` rather than plain `pt`, so the folder names need care.

**6. Write the other five translations.**
- This runs once the English file from step 2 is final.
- It follows the same voice and terms as the website (for example "subtítulos", "Untertitel", "字幕").

## Splitting the work
- Step 1 goes first, because everything else imports from it.
- After that, three subagents can run in parallel without touching the same files:
  - steps 2–3 (extension code)
  - step 4 (background error codes)
  - step 5 (manifest locale files)
- Step 6 runs once step 2's English file is final.
- Last, I check the integrated result: typecheck, tests, the extension build, and the website staying unchanged in the browser.

## Out of scope
- **Error messages from the shared transcription code**, such as "Could not connect to Deepgram" and "Deepgram didn't accept your API key". They're in English on the website too, so translating them is a separate follow-up for both apps.
- **Caption and transcript text.** It always shows what was said, or the translation you chose.

## What I can't check myself
The extension's pages need Chrome's extension APIs, which my browser pane doesn't have. I can confirm the typecheck, tests and build, but the actual check is yours: reload Heard, switch the language in settings, and look at the popup, side panel and caption box.

1	/**
2	 * Caption translation with Chrome's built-in, on-device Translator API
3	 * (developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/translator-api). Deepgram transcribes in the spoken language;
4	 * this turns that text into the viewer's language without any server or key: the model runs
5	 * in the browser and text never leaves it.
6	 *
7	 * Each language pair is a one-time download that Chrome only starts from a click, so the
8	 * settings UI calls `prepareTranslator` from its change handler, and the running session
9	 * reports a `download` issue when it meets a pair that isn't on the device yet.
10	 */
11	import { AUTO_LANGUAGE } from "./settings";
12	import type { CaptionState, TranscriptEvent, TranscriptLine, TranslationIssue } from "./types";
13	
14	type Availability = "unavailable" | "downloadable" | "downloading" | "available";
15	
16	interface ChromeTranslator {
17	  translate(text: string): Promise<string>;
18	  destroy(): void;
19	}
20	
21	interface ChromeTranslatorApi {
22	  availability(opts: { sourceLanguage: string; targetLanguage: string }): Promise<Availability>;
23	  create(opts: {
24	    sourceLanguage: string;
25	    targetLanguage: string;
26	    monitor?: (m: EventTarget) => void;
27	  }): Promise<ChromeTranslator>;
28	}
29	
30	function translatorApi(): ChromeTranslatorApi | null {
31	  const api = (globalThis as { Translator?: ChromeTranslatorApi }).Translator;
32	  return api && typeof api.create === "function" ? api : null;
33	}
34	
35	/** Whether this browser has Chrome's built-in translator. */
36	export function hasTranslator(): boolean {
37	  return translatorApi() !== null;
38	}
39	
40	/** Deepgram language code (`pt-BR`, `zh-TW`) → the code Chrome's translator expects (`pt`, `zh-Hant`). */
41	export function translatorCode(code: string): string {
42	  const c = code.trim().toLowerCase();
43	  if (c === "zh" || c.startsWith("zh-")) return /^zh-(tw|hk|mo|hant)/.test(c) ? "zh-Hant" : "zh";
44	  const base = c.split("-")[0] ?? c;
45	  return base === "iw" ? "he" : base;
46	}
47	
48	const translators = new Map<string, Promise<ChromeTranslator>>();
49	const pairKey = (source: string, target: string) => `${source}>${target}`;
50	
51	/** `no-api` when the browser has no built-in translator. */
52	export async function translatorAvailability(source: string, target: string): Promise<Availability | "no-api"> {
53	  const api = translatorApi();
54	  if (!api) return "no-api";
55	  try {
56	    // Some Chromium builds (embedded browsers) expose the API but never answer: treat that as no API.
57	    const timeout = new Promise<"no-api">((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve("no-api"), AVAILABILITY_TIMEOUT_MS));
58	    return await Promise.race([
59	      api.availability({ sourceLanguage: translatorCode(source), targetLanguage: translatorCode(target) }),
60	      timeout,
61	    ]);
62	  } catch {
63	    return "unavailable";
64	  }
65	}
66	
67	const AVAILABILITY_TIMEOUT_MS = 4000;
68	
69	/**
70	 * Start (or finish) the one-time download for a language pair. Call it straight from a click
71	 * or change handler: Chrome only downloads a model during a user gesture.
72	 * Resolves true once the pair is ready.
73	 */
74	export async function prepareTranslator(source: string, target: string, onProgress?: (fraction: number) => void): Promise<boolean> {
75	  const api = translatorApi();
76	  if (!api) return false;
77	  const s = translatorCode(source);
78	  const t = translatorCode(target);
79	  if (s === t) return true;
80	  const key = pairKey(s, t);
81	  const existing = translators.get(key);
82	  if (existing) return existing.then(() => true, () => false);
83	  const created = api.create({
84	    sourceLanguage: s,
85	    targetLanguage: t,
86	    monitor: (m) =>
87	      m.addEventListener("downloadprogress", (e) => onProgress?.(Number((e as Event & { loaded?: number }).loaded) || 0)),
88	  });
89	  translators.set(key, created);
90	  try {
91	    await created;
92	    return true;
93	  } catch {
94	    translators.delete(key);
95	    return false;
96	  }
97	}
98	
99	/** A ready translator for the pair, or the reason there isn't one. Never downloads. */
100	async function readyTranslator(source: string, target: string): Promise<ChromeTranslator | TranslationIssue["kind"]> {
101	  const key = pairKey(source, target);
102	  const existing = translators.get(key);
103	  if (existing) return existing.catch(() => "unsupported" as const);
104	  const availability = await translatorAvailability(source, target);
105	  if (availability === "no-api") return "no-api";
106	  if (availability === "unavailable") return "unsupported";
107	  if (availability !== "available") return "download";
108	  const api = translatorApi()!;
109	  const created = api.create({ sourceLanguage: source, targetLanguage: target });
110	  translators.set(key, created);
111	  try {
112	    return await created;
113	  } catch {
114	    translators.delete(key);
115	    return "download";
116	  }
117	}
118	
119	/** How long to wait before asking Chrome again about a pair that wasn't ready. */
120	const RECHECK_MS = 3000;
121	
122	/**
123	 * Follows a transcript's events and emits translations of its lines and live caption.
124	 * The caption is translated latest-wins, so a slow translation never queues up behind
125	 * a speaker: while one runs, only the newest caption text waits for the next turn.
126	 */
127	export class TranslationEngine {
128	  private spoken = AUTO_LANGUAGE;
129	  private target: string | null = null;
130	  private generation = 0;
131	  private issue: TranslationIssue | null = null;
132	  private notReadyUntil = new Map<string, number>();
133	  private captionBusy = false;
134	  private nextCaption: CaptionState | null = null;
135	
136	  constructor(private readonly emit: (event: TranscriptEvent) => void) {}
137	
138	  get active(): boolean {
139	    return this.target !== null;
140	  }
141	
142	  /** `spoken` is a Deepgram code or "multi"; `caption` is "" to keep the spoken language. */
143	  configure(spoken: string, caption: string): void {
144	    this.spoken = spoken || AUTO_LANGUAGE;
145	    const target = caption ? translatorCode(caption) : null;
146	    // A fixed spoken language that matches the caption language needs no translating.
147	    const next = target && this.spoken !== AUTO_LANGUAGE && translatorCode(this.spoken) === target ? null : target;
148	    if (next === this.target) return;
149	    this.target = next;
150	    this.generation += 1;
151	    this.issue = null;
152	    this.notReadyUntil.clear();
153	    this.emit({ type: "translation-config", target: next, issue: null });
154	  }
155	
156	  /** Feed every transcript event here. */
157	  handle(event: TranscriptEvent): void {
158	    if (!this.target) return;
159	    if (event.type === "line") void this.translateLine(event.line);
160	    else if (event.type === "caption") this.queueCaption(event.caption);
161	  }
162	
163	  private sourceFor(detected: string | undefined): string | null {
164	    const code = this.spoken === AUTO_LANGUAGE ? detected : this.spoken;
165	    return code ? translatorCode(code) : null;
166	  }
167	
168	  /** The translated text, the original when it's already in the target language, or null. */
169	  private async translate(text: string, detected: string | undefined): Promise<string | null> {
170	    const target = this.target;
171	    const source = this.sourceFor(detected);
172	    if (!target || !source) return null;
173	    if (source === target) return text;
174	    const key = pairKey(source, target);
175	    if ((this.notReadyUntil.get(key) ?? 0) > Date.now()) return null;
176	    const translator = await readyTranslator(source, target);
177	    if (typeof translator === "string") {
178	      this.notReadyUntil.set(key, Date.now() + RECHECK_MS);
179	      this.setIssue({ source, target, kind: translator });
180	      return null;
181	    }
182	    try {
183	      const out = await translator.translate(text);
184	      if (this.issue) this.setIssue(null);
185	      return out;
186	    } catch {
187	      return null;
188	    }
189	  }
190	
191	  private setIssue(issue: TranslationIssue | null) {
192	    const same =
193	      issue === this.issue ||
194	      (issue && this.issue && issue.kind === this.issue.kind && issue.source === this.issue.source && issue.target === this.issue.target);
195	    if (same) return;
196	    this.issue = issue;
197	    this.emit({ type: "translation-config", target: this.target, issue });
198	  }
199	
200	  private async translateLine(line: TranscriptLine) {
201	    const generation = this.generation;
202	    const target = this.target;
203	    const text = await this.translate(line.text, line.language);
204	    if (text === null || !target || generation !== this.generation) return;
205	    this.emit({ type: "line-translated", target, id: line.id, text });
206	  }
207	
208	  private queueCaption(caption: CaptionState) {
209	    this.nextCaption = caption;
210	    if (!this.captionBusy) void this.pumpCaptions();
211	  }
212	
213	  private async pumpCaptions() {
214	    this.captionBusy = true;
215	    try {
216	      while (this.nextCaption) {
217	        const caption = this.nextCaption;
218	        this.nextCaption = null;
219	        const generation = this.generation;
220	        const target = this.target;
221	        if (!target) break;
222	        const text = caption.text ? await this.translate(caption.text, caption.language) : "";

224	        // Untranslatable text shows as spoken rather than leaving an older translation up.
225	        this.emit({ type: "caption-translated", target, text: text ?? caption.text });
226	      }
227	    } finally {
228	      this.captionBusy = false;
229	    }
230	  }

content.text:
The extension now comes in the same six languages as the website: English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, German and Japanese. That covers the popup, the side panel, the caption box on the page, error messages, the toolbar tooltip and the extension's name and description in Chrome. Typecheck, tests (39 passing) and the extension build all pass. I haven't seen it in real Chrome yet, because my browser can't load extensions.

**How it works for you**
- By default it follows Chrome's language.
- In the side panel, **Settings → Interface language** lets you pick one. Every open view switches right away.
- The extension's name in `chrome://extensions` and the Web Store follows Chrome's language only. Chrome doesn't let the picker change it.

**What changed**
- **Shared translations:** the transcript, toolbar, status and caption settings text moved into `packages/shared` so the site and extension use one copy. The website is unchanged; I loaded the watch page in German and its labels still came through translated.
- **Extension text:** English is in [apps/extension/i18n/en.ts](apps/extension/i18n/en.ts). Subagents wrote the other five using the website's wording for each language. Each file is typed against English, so a missing string fails the typecheck.
- **Errors:** the background now sends codes like `tab_gone` instead of English sentences, and each view writes the sentence in its own language.
- **Name and description:** these are in `public/_locales/`. Portuguese uses Chrome's `pt_BR` folder. The Spanish and French descriptions are shortened to fit the Web Store's 132-character limit.

**Still in English:** errors from the transcription code itself, such as "Could not connect to Deepgram". They're English on the website too, so translating them is a follow-up for both apps.

**Not mine:** another session has uncommitted changes in the shared package (`LanguageSettings.tsx`, `icons.tsx` and a new `Select.tsx`). I left them alone, so a "commit everything" would include them.

**To check it:** reload Heard in `chrome://extensions` from `apps/extension/.output/chrome-mv3`. Switch Settings → Interface language to, say, Español, then look at the popup, the side panel and the caption box on a playing video.

This message doesn't say which two languages were requested, and Chrome usually writes it to the console on its own. It isn't the note my change adds. Two likely causes:

- **Deepgram guessed the wrong language for a phrase.** In my Spanish test, one phrase came back as Malay. Chrome can't translate Malay, so it refuses.
- **Chrome won't translate in the extension's hidden audio page at all.** If so, every pair gets the same refusal, and the fix is to move translation into the side panel.
